patient.name: Kwame Boateng
patient.setting: GP surgery, then upper GI cancer clinic
patient.complaint: Indigestion for 4 months that omeprazole has not helped, and 7 kg weight loss
background: H. pylori-positive duodenal ulcer 15 years ago, never had eradication completed
Drinks about 30 units of alcohol a week

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with an older smoker who has dyspepsia not responding to a PPI, weight loss and anaemia, sometimes with a Virchow's node, Krukenberg tumour or Sister Mary Joseph nodule as the giveaway.

points: He fills up quickly, feels sick and has lost **7 kg**.
Wife says he looks pale and tired.

steps.lead: Kwame's dyspepsia, nausea and **weight loss**, plus **failure of a PPI**, are the alarm pattern for gastric cancer.
He is a heavy **smoker** and drinker with untreated **H. pylori**, which alone raises his risk about **6-fold**.

visual.title: Where Kwame's pain and mass are
visual.caption: Epigastric discomfort and a vague, hard epigastric mass on deep palpation.

points: No left supraclavicular node, no ascites, no periumbilical nodules.
No jaundice; rectal exam: no melaena.

steps.lead: Kwame has none of the late signs yet, which matters: **Virchow's node**, ascites or nodules would mean spread.

steps.q: If Kwame had a hard lump above his left clavicle, what would it be called?
steps.r: A palpable left supraclavicular node is **Virchow's node**; finding it is **Troisier's sign**.

steps.lead: Kwame's tumour will almost certainly be an **adenocarcinoma**; signet ring cells on biopsy would mark the diffuse type.
If Kwame's tumour eroded through the stomach wall, he would **perforate**: sudden pain, peritonitis and air under the diaphragm.

visual.title: Erect chest X-ray in perforation
visual.caption: Free air under the diaphragm (pneumoperitoneum) means a perforated viscus.

steps.text: This is what a gastric perforation would look like on an erect chest X-ray.
Do not keep doubling the PPI. **Dyspepsia that fails a PPI** in an older patient with weight loss needs an endoscopy, not more acid suppression.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?' (urgent OGD with biopsy) and then staging questions (CT chest, abdomen and pelvis; endoscopic ultrasound).

steps.title: Kwame's bloods
steps.text: Microcytic iron deficiency anaemia from slow bleeding from the tumour.

visual.title: Kwame's haemoglobin
visual.label: Kwame 96
visual.caption: Iron deficiency anaemia in an older man is upper or lower GI cancer until proven otherwise.

steps.q: What is the most appropriate first investigation for Kwame?
o: Urgent upper GI endoscopy with biopsy
steps.r: **Urgent (2-week wait) OGD with biopsy** sees and samples the lesion. CT stages it later; tumour markers do not diagnose.

steps.lead: Kwame is over 55 with weight loss and upper abdominal symptoms, so he goes on the **2-week wait** for OGD.

points: OGD: ulcerated, heaped-up mass in the **gastric antrum**.
Histology: **adenocarcinoma, intestinal type**; H. pylori present.

steps.lead: Kwame's **endoscopy and biopsy** prove the diagnosis; nothing else can give histology.

steps.title: From symptom to stage
nodes: EUS for local depth and nodes

steps.lead: Kwame's **CT CAP** shows no liver or lung metastases; **EUS** shows the tumour through the muscle wall with one local node (T3 N1 M0).

steps.text: CT is for **staging**, not diagnosis. A barium meal or tumour markers never replace endoscopy with biopsy.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate management?' where the stage decides: gastrectomy for early disease, perioperative FLOT then surgery for locally advanced, palliative chemotherapy or stenting for metastatic disease.

steps.title: Stage decides treatment
nodes: Upper GI MDT reviews CT and EUS
Obstruction or bleeding: stent, urgent admission

steps.q: Kwame is T3 N1 M0 and fit. What is the best plan?
steps.r: Locally advanced, resectable disease: **perioperative FLOT** chemotherapy around surgery.

steps.lead: Kwame has **locally advanced** disease, so he gets **FLOT** chemotherapy before and after his operation.
After FLOT, Kwame's antral tumour is removed by **partial gastrectomy**; a Billroth I joins the stomach remnant to the duodenum.

visual.title: Kwame's weight through treatment
visual.caption: Weight falls with chemotherapy and surgery, then starts to recover with dietitian support.

steps.lead: Kwame's path follows the **2-week wait** upper GI pathway and the **FLOT** perioperative regimen.

steps.text: After gastrectomy, food rushing into the small bowel causes **early dumping**: cramps, sweating and palpitations within 30 minutes of eating.

steps.lead: Had Kwame presented vomiting old food from **gastric outlet obstruction**, an **endoscopic stent** would relieve it, with urgent admission.
If Kwame later develops liver or peritoneal spread, treatment becomes **palliative chemotherapy**.

steps.text: Do not offer surgery alone for locally advanced disease. Perioperative chemotherapy improves survival, and metastatic disease is not resected.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: how H. pylori or pernicious anaemia leads to cancer, intestinal versus diffuse type, and how it spreads to Virchow's node or the ovaries.

steps.lead: Kwame's long-standing **H. pylori** inflamed his stomach for years, causing atrophy and intestinal metaplasia before the cancer.

steps.title: From infection to intestinal-type cancer
steps.caption: Each step takes years; this is why eradication matters.

steps.lead: Kwame has the **intestinal** type, which forms a mass. The **diffuse** signet ring type infiltrates the wall and has a worse prognosis.

steps.q: Why is Virchow's node on the LEFT side?
o: Haematogenous spread via the portal vein
Lymph drains via the thoracic duct into the left neck
The stomach lies on the left
steps.r: Abdominal lymph drains through the **thoracic duct**, which empties at the left subclavian-jugular junction.

steps.lead: This is how Kwame's cancer could spread: lymph to **Virchow's node**; signet ring cells across the peritoneum to the ovaries in women (**Krukenberg**).

steps.text: **Krukenberg** tumours are ovarian metastases, not a primary ovarian cancer. Signet ring cells in an ovary should make you look at the stomach.

mcq.q: What is the most common histological type of gastric cancer?
mcq.r: **Adenocarcinoma**; signet ring cells mark the diffuse subtype.

mcq.q: Roughly how much does H. pylori increase gastric cancer risk?
mcq.r: About **6-fold**, an extremely strong risk factor.
**Bilateral ovarian metastases**, classically from signet ring gastric cancer.

mcq.q: What is a Sister Mary Joseph nodule?
Which disease of gastric mucosal hypertrophy with achlorhydria raises gastric cancer risk?
mcq.r: **Menetrier's disease**: hypertrophic gastric folds with achlorhydria.

mcq.q: What is the gold standard investigation for gastric cancer?
Which test assesses the local depth of invasion?
mcq.r: **EUS** stages local invasion; CT CAP looks for distant spread.

mcq.q: Which chemotherapy regimen is used perioperatively for locally advanced gastric cancer?
Which complication causes cramps and sweating soon after eating post-gastrectomy?
mcq.r: **Early dumping**: rapid emptying of food into the small bowel.

mcq.q: Through which structure does gastric cancer reach Virchow's node?
mcq.r: Lymphatic spread via the **thoracic duct** to the left supraclavicular fossa.

technique.stem: A 71 year old man has a 3 month history of epigastric discomfort, early satiety and 8 kg weight loss. Lansoprazole has not helped. He smokes 20 cigarettes a day. He is pale, and there is a hard lymph node in the left supraclavicular fossa.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Diagnosis with upper GI symptoms: look for **alarm features**.

clues: hard lymph node in the left supraclavicular fossa
steps.x: Weight loss, PPI failure, smoking and a **Virchow's node**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Gastric adenocarcinoma** with lymphatic spread.

elim: Achalasia causes dysphagia to solids and liquids, not a Virchow's node.
Chronic pancreatitis gives pain radiating to the back, steatorrhoea and diabetes.
Hiatus hernia causes reflux, not weight loss and a hard node.
Peptic ulcer responds to PPI and does not cause lymphadenopathy.

steps.x: **C. Gastric adenocarcinoma.** Virchow's node = Troisier's sign = gastric cancer until proven otherwise.

technique.stem: A 63 year old woman has a 2 month history of upper abdominal pain and 5 kg unintentional weight loss. She has pernicious anaemia. Her GP finds epigastric tenderness. Her haemoglobin is 98 g/L (115–165).
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
o: Urgent upper GI endoscopy with biopsy

steps.x: **Initial** investigation for suspected upper GI cancer.
Over 55, weight loss and upper abdominal pain, a risk factor and anaemia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **2-week wait OGD with biopsy**.

elim: CT stages after the diagnosis is made.
FIT is for suspected colorectal cancer.
H. pylori testing is for uncomplicated dyspepsia without alarm features.
Tumour markers are not diagnostic.

steps.x: **E. Urgent OGD with biopsy.** See it, sample it.

technique.stem: A 69 year old man has biopsy-proven gastric adenocarcinoma. CT chest, abdomen and pelvis shows multiple liver metastases and peritoneal deposits. He is eating and drinking normally, with no vomiting or bleeding. He is independent and wants active treatment.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate management?

steps.x: Management: **stage** first.
Metastatic disease, no obstruction, fit and keen.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Palliative chemotherapy**.

elim: Gastrectomy is for early, resectable disease.
Stenting is for obstruction; he is eating normally.
Eradication does not treat established cancer.
Perioperative FLOT is for locally advanced, non-metastatic disease.

steps.x: **D. Palliative chemotherapy.** Metastatic = palliative.

technique.stem: A 74 year old woman with long-standing pernicious anaemia on vitamin B12 injections is found to have a gastric adenocarcinoma. Biopsies of the surrounding mucosa show atrophic gastritis with intestinal metaplasia. Her gastric pH is high.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism linking her pernicious anaemia to the cancer?

steps.x: A **mechanism** linking a risk factor to the cancer.
Autoimmune destruction of parietal cells, no acid, metaplasia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Chronic atrophic gastritis and achlorhydria** drive metaplasia and cancer.

elim: Bile reflux is a post-surgical problem, not the pernicious anaemia link.
Pernicious anaemia causes too little acid, not too much.
Iron deficiency is a result of bleeding, not the cause.
B12 replacement is treatment and is not carcinogenic.

steps.x: **A. Achlorhydria with atrophic gastritis.** Same road as H. pylori: atrophy, metaplasia, cancer.

practice.stem: A 68 year old man has a 4 month history of epigastric discomfort and nausea despite 8 weeks of omeprazole. He has lost 6 kg and fills up quickly. He smokes and had H. pylori infection in the past. His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 94 bpm and BP 124/72 mmHg. There is a firm epigastric mass.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Dyspepsia failing a PPI, weight loss, iron deficiency anaemia and an epigastric mass in an older smoker with past H. pylori is gastric cancer. Oesophageal cancer presents with dysphagia.

steps.x: Diagnosis: are there **alarm features**?
PPI failure, weight loss, early satiety, risk factor, mass; labs show iron deficiency.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Gastric adenocarcinoma**.

elim: Oesophageal cancer presents with progressive dysphagia.
Pancreatic cancer gives painless jaundice or back pain.
Peptic ulcer responds to PPI and does not cause a mass.
Zollinger-Ellison causes multiple ulcers and diarrhoea, not an epigastric mass.

steps.x: **A. Gastric adenocarcinoma.** PPI failure plus weight loss = scope it.

practice.stem: A 70 year old man has a 3 month history of indigestion, anorexia and 9 kg weight loss. He has smoked for 50 years. An OGD shows an ulcerated mass in the gastric body, and biopsy confirms adenocarcinoma. His GP examines him again.
practice.q: Which is the most likely additional finding on examination?
practice.e: Lymphatic spread through the thoracic duct gives a hard left supraclavicular node (Virchow's node, Troisier's sign). Courvoisier and Murphy are biliary signs.

steps.x: A 'most likely finding' in a patient with proven gastric cancer: think of the signs of spread.

clues: ulcerated mass in the gastric body
steps.x: Proven, probably advanced gastric adenocarcinoma: look for its classic sign of lymphatic spread.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Virchow's node** in the left supraclavicular fossa.

elim: Grey Turner's is flank bruising in pancreatitis.
Murphy's sign is acute cholecystitis.
A palpable gallbladder with jaundice is pancreatic head cancer (Courvoisier).
Spider naevi suggest chronic liver disease, not gastric cancer spread.

steps.x: **B. Hard left supraclavicular node.** Troisier's sign.

practice.stem: A 49 year old woman has abdominal distension, 4 months of epigastric pain and early satiety, and weight loss. Ultrasound shows bilateral solid ovarian masses and ascites. Biopsy of an ovarian mass shows mucin-filled signet ring cells. Her CA-125 is mildly raised.
practice.q: Which is the most likely primary tumour?
practice.e: Bilateral ovarian metastases containing signet ring cells are a Krukenberg tumour, classically from diffuse gastric adenocarcinoma. Epigastric pain and early satiety point to the stomach.

steps.x: It asks for the **primary**, so these masses are metastases.
Bilateral, solid, signet ring: **Krukenberg**. Upper GI symptoms. CA-125 rises with any peritoneal disease.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Gastric adenocarcinoma** (diffuse, signet ring type).

elim: Colorectal cancer can spread to the ovaries but there are no bowel symptoms; gastric is classic.
Endometrial cancer presents with postmenopausal bleeding.
Primary serous carcinoma does not show signet ring cells.
Pancreatic cancer gives jaundice or back pain.

steps.x: **C. Gastric adenocarcinoma.** Krukenberg = signet ring cells from the stomach.

practice.stem: A 61 year old man has a gastric adenocarcinoma diagnosed on OGD biopsy. The surrounding mucosa shows chronic active gastritis, atrophy and intestinal metaplasia, and curved Gram-negative rods are seen on the mucosal surface. His pulse rate is 82 bpm and BP 136/84 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause of his cancer?
practice.e: H. pylori causes chronic gastritis, atrophy and intestinal metaplasia, the precursor of intestinal-type gastric adenocarcinoma, with about a 6-fold increased risk.

steps.x: A cause question: the organism behind the cancer.
The Correa cascade with a curved Gram-negative rod on the gastric mucosa.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Helicobacter pylori**.

elim: Campylobacter causes enteritis, not gastric cancer.
Hepatitis B causes hepatocellular carcinoma.
HPV causes cervical, anal and oropharyngeal cancers.
Whipple's disease affects the small bowel, not gastric cancer.

steps.x: **B. H. pylori.** About 6-fold increased risk.

practice.stem: A 66 year old woman has 5 months of epigastric pain, vomiting and 10 kg weight loss. Her abdomen is distended with shifting dullness. There is a hard, non-tender nodule at the umbilicus. Her temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 102 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg. OGD confirms a gastric adenocarcinoma.
practice.q: Which is the most likely explanation for the umbilical nodule?
practice.e: A hard periumbilical nodule in gastric cancer with ascites is a Sister Mary Joseph nodule, a subcutaneous metastasis. Cullen's sign is bruising, not a nodule.

steps.x: Explain a sign in a patient with known gastric cancer.

clues: hard, non-tender nodule at the umbilicus
steps.x: Ascites and a hard umbilical lump in advanced gastric cancer.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Sister Mary Joseph nodule**: a metastatic deposit.

elim: Caput medusae is dilated veins in portal hypertension.
Cullen's sign is periumbilical bruising in pancreatitis or ectopic pregnancy.
A hernia is soft and reducible with a cough impulse.
A urachal cyst is congenital and midline below the umbilicus.

steps.x: **C. Metastatic deposit.** Sister Mary Joseph nodule = advanced disease.

practice.stem: A 72 year old man with known gastric adenocarcinoma awaiting surgery has sudden severe epigastric pain that spread across his abdomen. His abdomen is rigid with absent bowel sounds. His temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 118 bpm and BP 96/60 mmHg. Erect chest X-ray (see item resources).
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Sudden pain, peritonitis and free air under the diaphragm in a patient with gastric cancer is perforation of the tumour. Pancreatitis does not cause pneumoperitoneum.

steps.x: Acute complication of known gastric cancer; look at the X-ray.
Peritonitis plus **free air** on the film.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Gastric perforation**.

elim: Mesenteric ischaemia gives pain out of proportion without free air.
Pancreatitis does not cause pneumoperitoneum.
Outlet obstruction gives vomiting of old food, not peritonitis.
A bleed gives haematemesis or melaena and shock, not free air.

steps.x: **D. Gastric perforation.** Free air = perforated viscus.

practice.stem: A 64 year old man has a 6 week history of upper abdominal pain, reflux and 4 kg unintentional weight loss. He has no dysphagia. His pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 132/80 mmHg. Examination is normal apart from pallor.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
practice.e: Aged 55 or over with weight loss and upper abdominal pain or reflux needs a 2-week wait OGD with biopsy. CT and EUS stage the cancer once it is confirmed.

steps.x: **Initial** investigation with alarm features.
Over 55, weight loss and upper GI symptoms, plus microcytic anaemia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Urgent OGD with biopsy** on the 2-week wait.

elim: Barium swallow cannot biopsy and is for motility problems.
CT stages after diagnosis.
EUS stages local depth after diagnosis.
A breath test is for uncomplicated dyspepsia without alarm features.

steps.x: **D. OGD with biopsy.** Alarm features skip test-and-treat.

practice.stem: A 66 year old woman has an antral gastric adenocarcinoma confirmed on OGD biopsy. She is fit and the upper GI team are considering treatment options. She has no neurological symptoms.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation to stage her cancer?
practice.e: Staging of gastric cancer is by CT chest, abdomen and pelvis for distant spread, with endoscopic ultrasound for local invasion.

steps.x: Diagnosis is made; the question is **staging**.
Proven cancer, needs stage to choose treatment; no reason to image the brain.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **CT chest, abdomen and pelvis**.

elim: Barium adds nothing once histology is known.
MRI brain is not routine without neurological signs.
The diagnosis is already proven.
Ultrasound misses lung and nodal disease.

steps.x: **B. CT CAP.** Then EUS for local depth.

practice.stem: A 62 year old man has a small antral gastric adenocarcinoma found on OGD. CT chest, abdomen and pelvis shows no spread, and endoscopic ultrasound shows early disease with no nodal involvement. He is fit for surgery.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
practice.e: Early gastric cancer in a fit patient is treated by surgical resection (gastrectomy). Chemotherapy is added for locally advanced disease; palliative chemotherapy is for metastatic disease.

steps.x: Treatment depends on **stage**.

clues: early disease with no nodal involvement
steps.x: Early, localised, resectable, fit.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Gastrectomy**.

elim: Stenting palliates obstruction.
Eradication does not cure cancer.
Palliative chemotherapy is for metastatic disease.
Radiotherapy alone is not curative treatment for gastric cancer.

steps.x: **E. Gastrectomy.** Early = cut it out.

practice.stem: A 58 year old woman has a gastric adenocarcinoma. Staging CT and endoscopic ultrasound show the tumour invading through the muscularis propria with two involved local nodes and no distant metastases. Her temperature is 36.5°C, pulse rate 78 bpm and BP 128/78 mmHg. She is fit.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
practice.e: Locally advanced, non-metastatic gastric cancer is treated with perioperative chemotherapy (FLOT) around gastrectomy. Surgery alone undertreats it.

steps.x: Stage-based treatment.
Locally advanced (T3 N1 M0), resectable, fit.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Perioperative FLOT** with gastrectomy.

elim: She is fit with curable disease.
No obstruction to relieve.
Surgery alone undertreats locally advanced disease.
Palliative chemotherapy is for metastatic disease; she has none.

steps.x: **E. Perioperative chemotherapy and gastrectomy.** Locally advanced = FLOT sandwich.

practice.stem: A 76 year old man with metastatic gastric adenocarcinoma of the antrum has 5 days of vomiting undigested food several hours after meals. He cannot keep fluids down. His pulse rate is 104 bpm and BP 104/66 mmHg. A succussion splash is present.
practice.q: After fluid and electrolyte resuscitation, which is the most appropriate management?
practice.e: Malignant gastric outlet obstruction in metastatic disease is palliated with an endoscopic stent after resuscitation. Curative surgery and perioperative chemotherapy are not appropriate with metastases.

steps.x: Emergency symptom control in advanced disease.

clues: metastatic gastric adenocarcinoma of the antrum
steps.x: **Gastric outlet obstruction**; labs show hypokalaemic, hypochloraemic alkalosis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Resuscitate, then **endoscopic stent**.

elim: Curative resection is not done with metastatic disease.
Eradication does nothing for obstruction.
Long-term NG feeding does not relieve the blockage.
Perioperative FLOT is for non-metastatic disease.

steps.x: **B. Endoscopic stenting.** Palliate the obstruction.

practice.stem: A 65 year old man with gastric adenocarcinoma has a hard, non-tender lymph node in the left supraclavicular fossa. CT shows no lung or liver metastases. Fine needle aspiration of the node shows adenocarcinoma cells.
practice.q: Which is the most likely route by which the cancer reached this node?
o: Haematogenous spread via the portal vein
Lymphatic spread via the thoracic duct
practice.e: Abdominal lymph drains through the thoracic duct into the left subclavian-jugular junction, so gastric cancer spreads to Virchow's node in the left supraclavicular fossa.

steps.x: A mechanism of **spread** question.
Nodal disease without blood-borne spread.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Lymphatic spread via the thoracic duct**.

elim: Direct invasion would not skip to the neck.
Portal spread goes to the liver first; the liver is clear.
Perineural spread follows nerves locally.
Transcoelomic spread seeds the peritoneum and ovaries (Krukenberg).

steps.x: **C. Thoracic duct.** Left side because that is where the duct drains.

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: name the type and the subtype marker.

points.why: Squamous cell carcinoma is oesophageal, not gastric.
Infiltrates without a discrete mass; worse prognosis.

prompts.q: What are the risk factors for gastric cancer?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the stem will plant one; H. pylori is the big one.

prompts.q: How does gastric cancer usually present?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: dyspepsia plus an alarm feature.

prompts.q: What are the late signs of gastric cancer, with their eponyms?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: each eponym is a location of spread.

points.p: Virchow's node: left supraclavicular node (Troisier's sign)
Sister Mary Joseph nodule: periumbilical metastasis

prompts.q: Which acute complication can gastric cancer cause and what does it show?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: sudden pain plus a film.

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the answer is nearly always OGD with biopsy.

points.p: Urgent (2-week wait) upper GI endoscopy (OGD) with biopsy
For weight loss, upper abdominal pain, age over 55
points.why: NICE: 55 or over with weight loss plus upper abdominal pain, reflux or dyspepsia.

points.p: Histology may show signet ring cells

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: CT for distant, EUS for local.

points.why: Distant spread to liver, lung, peritoneum.
Depth through the wall and local nodes.

prompts.q: How is gastric cancer treated at each stage?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the stage in the stem decides the answer.

prompts.q: What surgery is used, its classic complication, and the emergency options?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: name the operation and what goes wrong.

points.p: Billroth I: partial gastrectomy with gastroduodenal anastomosis

points.why: Rapid emptying into small bowel after meals.

points.p: Outlet obstruction or bleeding need urgent hospital management

prompts.q: Why do H. pylori and pernicious anaemia increase gastric cancer risk?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the sequence from gastritis to cancer.

points.p: Intestinal metaplasia, precursor to intestinal-type adenocarcinoma

prompts.q: How do intestinal and diffuse types differ, and how does gastric cancer spread?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: link each sign to its route.

points.p: Diffuse (signet ring) infiltrates without a mass; worse prognosis
points.why: Intestinal type forms a mass and links to H. pylori.

points.p: Virchow's node: lymphatic spread via thoracic duct
points.why: Drains to the left supraclavicular fossa.

points.why: Signet ring cells seed the ovaries.

glossary.adenocarcinoma: Cancer arising from glandular epithelium; the main type of gastric cancer.
glossary.signet ring cell: Cancer cell full of mucin that pushes the nucleus to one side, like a signet ring.
glossary.diffuse type: Gastric cancer of signet ring cells that infiltrates the wall without a discrete mass.
glossary.intestinal type: Gland-forming gastric cancer arising from intestinal metaplasia, linked to H. pylori.
glossary.linitis plastica: Stiff, thickened 'leather bottle' stomach from diffuse-type infiltration.
glossary.H. pylori: Helicobacter pylori: curved Gram-negative bacterium causing gastritis, ulcers and gastric cancer.
glossary.pernicious anaemia: Autoimmune destruction of parietal cells causing B12 deficiency and achlorhydria.
glossary.atrophic gastritis: Chronic inflammation that thins the stomach lining and loses acid-producing glands.
glossary.intestinal metaplasia: Stomach lining replaced by intestinal-type cells; a precancerous change.
glossary.Menetrier's disease: Rare disease of giant gastric folds with protein loss and low acid.
glossary.early satiety: Feeling full after eating only a small amount.
glossary.PPI: Proton pump inhibitor, such as omeprazole, that blocks stomach acid secretion.
glossary.Virchow's node: Enlarged left supraclavicular lymph node from abdominal cancer spread.
glossary.Troisier's sign: Finding a palpable Virchow's node on examination.
glossary.Krukenberg tumour: Metastasis to the ovaries, usually bilateral, classically from signet ring gastric cancer.
glossary.Sister Mary Joseph nodule: Hard nodule at the umbilicus from metastatic abdominal or pelvic cancer.
glossary.pneumoperitoneum: Free air in the abdominal cavity, usually from a perforated viscus.
glossary.OGD: Oesophagogastroduodenoscopy: a camera passed into the oesophagus, stomach and duodenum.
glossary.2-week wait: NHS urgent suspected cancer referral, seen within two weeks.
glossary.EUS: Endoscopic ultrasound: ultrasound probe on an endoscope to stage local depth and nodes.
glossary.CT CAP: CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis, used to look for distant spread.
glossary.MDT: Multidisciplinary team meeting that agrees cancer treatment.
glossary.gastrectomy: Surgical removal of all or part of the stomach.
glossary.Billroth I: Partial gastrectomy with the stomach remnant joined directly to the duodenum.
glossary.dumping syndrome: Symptoms after eating post-gastrectomy as food rushes into the small bowel.
glossary.FLOT: Chemotherapy of 5-FU, leucovorin, oxaliplatin and docetaxel given around gastric cancer surgery.
glossary.perioperative chemotherapy: Chemotherapy given both before and after an operation.
glossary.palliative chemotherapy: Chemotherapy to control symptoms and extend life, not to cure.
glossary.gastric outlet obstruction: Blockage at the pylorus causing vomiting of undigested food.
glossary.succussion splash: Sloshing sound over the stomach when shaken, from retained fluid in outlet obstruction.
glossary.thoracic duct: Main lymph vessel draining most of the body into the left subclavian vein.
glossary.transcoelomic spread: Spread of cancer cells across a body cavity such as the peritoneum.
glossary.microcytic anaemia: Anaemia with small red cells, usually from iron deficiency.
